newsitem.title: INDIA: OPINION - Indian Budget - Standard Chartered.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Indian Budget - Standard Chartered.

text.p: INDIAN BUDGET:A STEP IN THE RIGHT DIRECTION - An
analysis of the Indian budget 1997/98 by Standard Chartered Bank.

The 1997/98 federal budget lived up to market expectations with the introduction of several measures to boost capital markets. The announcements sparked a bull run in the benchmark BSE index, causing it to rise by over six percent.
Moreover, the positive sentiment is expected to continue in coming weeks with further gains in the stock market expected.

Foreign and domestic investors will benefit from the budget helping to improve confidence in the government's economic strategy. Corporate profitability should also show signs of improvement in coming months due to the reductions in corporate taxes.

Further out, investors will need to see signs of an improving economy, lower levels of real interest, and diminishing political uncertainty before the stock market yields sustained gains with volatility continuing in the meantime.

The moves towards capital account convertibility of the rupee should also boost sentiment in the short term with Chidambaram's stating that the time had come for "preparatory work" towards such a move.

The setting up of a panel to pave the way for convertibility is a positive measure that will be well received by foreign investors given that rupee convertibility remains a major obstacle to foreign investment.
However, this remains only the first step in the right direction with any significant measures not expected in the near term given that the criteria for convertibility remain largely unfulfilled.

Foreign currency reserves though adequate ($19.5 billion equivalent to 5.2 months' import cover) will need to rise significantly before a move to free up the rupee on the capital account can be implemented.

The inflationary outlook which is another pre-requisite, is not expected to improve in the medium term, whilst an imprvement on the trade front, another necessary factor, is not expected anytime soon.
Overall, the budget is seen as market-friendly and will provide a kickstart to the economy in the short term reassuring investors of the government's commitment to reform and liberalisation.
However, doubts remain over the government's ability to rein in the fiscal deficit to comply with targets, particularly given the large scale reduction in taxes.
Although this will be balanced to some extent by a wider base of tax collections the assumptions on revenue raising may be a bit too optimistic.

Moreover, the target of 48 billion rupees for divestment revenue seems excessive given the inability to meet previous targets and political opposition to a rigorous sale of state assets. Infrastructure remains a top priority but the government does not seem to have done enough in this budget to fuel signiificant investment in this area.
Therefore, once the initial euphoria wears off, the government will need to put words into actions and provide further new measures or risk losing the market's newfound optimism.
(The opinions expressed in this article reflect the views of the author only. They should not be taken as reflecting the views of Reuters)
